title: Where are we?
author: Calm-You-4757
selftext:
We're a three-person family run studio, and we've been building WORLDS: Anthropos for five years. It's a top-down sci-fi RPG built in GameMaker Studio 2. Our Steam wishlist page is up now, and we're expecting to launch Nov 2027. Our AI workflow has changed a lot over those five years, so we wanted to share what it actually looked like up until now.

**Where we started**  
This was our first project together. This is where everyone except the lead dev, learned to code, and even the lead devs knowledge has expanded quite a lot since our beginning. We picked up everything from YouTube tutorials and whatever we could find online when we first started, even the art was 100% hand-made. During that time AI was in it's baby stages, and we had not yet deemed it viable for use. So, AI didn't come into play until all of our base mechanics were solidified (mostly bug free).

**Art and animation**  
After a very long time of dabbling, we finally landed on our workflows. We now use ComfyUI with a LoRA trained on our art style to generate base assets, andf or existing characters, we sketch the pose needed, then give ChatGPT the sketched pose and the character's model sheet to generate the new pose. We use the ChatGPT workflow for key frames in our animations, and for some concept art. The in-between frames for the animations are then done by hand, and the AI frames are tweaked to match our style and keep the characters consistency.

A great example of our ChatGPT workflow is the main character herself! Her base four directional run are all done by hand beginning to end, whereas her three quarter run animations were done using the exact steps in the example above. We generated a base version of the poses/frames with ChatGPT, then we edited her suit, colors, size, etc., then filled in the rest of the animation frames by hand.

Consistency is the hard part, and that's why we always hand edit our assets after the initial generation. ChatGPT will often lose details, or add things that weren't there, the biggest struggle being color and lighting consistency! With ComfyUI, it's very similar, assets are often too light, don't always stay consistent with the art style, and overall need tweaking and editing to match our visions.

**Code**  
We use Claude in collaboration with Obsidian. Obsidian allows Claude to track our game files, plans, and notes, helping Claude "remember" our existing codebase. A lot of our code was written before we brought AI in, so this memory setup matters a lot for our workflow, or any workflow with mass amounts of code. You can also link your GitHub and upload your code there instead! As you can imagine, this also requires maintenance to make sure it's always the most recent and updated version so we prevent any possible bugs or misunderstandings.

Our workflow went through many stages, and here's a few:

* **Bug fixer only.** Before we had Claude with the memory system we used good ol' ChatGPT. This caused a lot of new bugs. It was good at writing new snippets, which we had to splice into our existing code by hand, and after hours of arguing it was good at fixing some of our bugs.
* **Step back.** Because we weren't skilled enough yet for our vision, and AI wasn't the aid we needed yet we worked on other projects. During this time we learned much more about code and how to use AI.
* **Now.** We've switched almost completely to AI-written code (or vibe coding as they say). Every idea for mechanics, characters, and feel is ours, but Claude writes the new code.

An example of our recent workflow would be our recent upgrade system (Which can be seen in newer gameplay shorts). It built on our existing menu code, but the upgrade code itself was written by Claude. Even with a drastically improved workflow, we hit snags every now and then (Not as bad as in the past though)! We had a broken toggle between viewing a weapon and upgrading it, our exit game button stopped working, and a few smaller bugs. Because the lead dev, Anthony, tracks every change the AI makes and still understands our pipelines and logic, he can point to where the problem most likely is and fix it with the AI, rarely having to fix anything by hand. Even when using AI it's important to have an idea of what's what, and how everything works.

**Review**  
Anthony reviews all AI output and pulls in the rest of the team for harder questions like when we use AI to help with dialogue, priority lists, and other aspects of our development. Because we review everything, it's almost never the way it started.

**What surprised us**  
How hard it was to start our game development. People talk about AI like a cheat code, but there's a real learning curve, especially when you're not making the whole game with it from beginning to end. Our approach has gone through many stages, different tools, and even different projects, just for us to end up where we are now!

**Credits**  
we use AI tools for early concept drafts, and to aid in writing new code. All in-game art is made by lead-dev, Anthony, and Maya is voiced by voice actor Autumn Teague.  
We're happy to answer questions about any part of our pipeline, and game!

**Question for you:** How do you improve your workflows as a small team? How have you used AI to help mitigate the workflow and make it more viable to release a game in a shorter amount of time?

comments.author: Xinnobun
comments.body: A robot that can run quickly, attack and kill is nothing short of nightmare material.
